parts.problem_md:
The *R*<sub>f</sub> values of three different pigments are shown in the table.

| pigment | *R*<sub>f</sub> value |
|---|---|
| P | 0.43 |
| Q | 0.57 |
| R | 0.75 |

A student carries out chromatography on an unknown sample. The resulting chromatogram is shown below

![Chromatogram. Baseline at 0.0 cm. Solvent front at 7.0 cm. One sample spot at 3.0 cm above baseline. Ruler shown 0.0–7.0 cm.](assets/001-chromatogram-baseline-at-0-0-cm-solvent-front-at.png)

What is the identity of the unknown pigment?
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- To identify the pigment, you must calculate the *R*<sub>f</sub> value of the unknown spot using the formula:

$R_{f}=\frac{\mathrm{distance} \mathrm{travelled} \mathrm{by} \mathrm{substance}}{\mathrm{distance} \mathrm{travelled} \mathrm{by} \mathrm{solvent}}$

- Using the diagram:

![Chromatogram. Horizontal baseline at 0.0 cm. Horizontal solvent front line at 7.0 cm. One spot at 3.0 cm above baseline. Vertical arrows show 3.0 cm (spot) and 7.0 cm (solvent front).](assets/002-chromatogram-horizontal-baseline-at-0-0-cm-horiz.png)

- Distance travelled by substance = 3.0 cm
- Distance travelled by solvent (solvent front) = 7.0 cm

$R_{f}=\frac{3.0}{7.0}=0.428..=0.43$

- Comparing this to the table, the unknown sample matches **pigment P **

> **[exam-tip]**
> Always measure the distance from the **baseline to the centre of the spot**, not the top or bottom. Using the centre of the spot ensures accurate **Rf values** and avoids losing marks for measurement errors.

parts.problem_md:
**Extended tier only**

Four different dyes labelled P, Q, R and S produced the chromatograms as shown below.

![q2-hard-mcq-12-2-separation-purification-cie-igcse-chemistry](assets/003-q2-hard-mcq-12-2-separation-purification-cie-igc.png)

Which dye has an *R*<sub>f</sub> value of 0.7?
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is**** A**** because:**

- Measure the distance from the baseline to each sample spot.
- Measure the distance from the baseline to the solvent front.
- Use the equation for the retention factor: *R*<sub>f</sub> = $\frac{distancetravelledbyspot}{distancetravelledbysolventfront}$
- Determine which sample spot produces an answer of 0.7.

**B**,** C **and** D **are incorrect as these dyes do not produce an *R*<sub>f </sub>value of 0.7.

parts.problem_md: A yellow solid, W is soluble in water. Which method of separation can be used to obtain the solid W from an aqueous solution?
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is**** D**** because:**

- Crystallisation is a separation technique used to separate a **soluble solid** from a  solution.
- It involves evaporating the solution to a much smaller volume and then leaving it to cool.
- As the solution cools, crystals of the solid form.

**A **is incorrect as neutralisation is the reaction between an **acid **and a **base** and is not a separation technique.

**B **is incorrect as chromatography is useful for separating a mixture of **dissolved** substances.

**C** is incorrect as distillation is used to separate a **pure liquid **from a **solution **or a **mixture **of liquids.

parts.problem_md:
**Extended tier only**

It is important that substances used in the synthesis of medicines are pure as impurities in these products can be detrimental to our health. Samples of pure and impure paracetamol were analysed using chromatography. The resulting chromatogram is shown below.

![q4-hard-mcq-12-2-separation-purification-cie-igcse-chemistry](assets/004-q4-hard-mcq-12-2-separation-purification-cie-igc.png)

The impure sample of paracetamol was contaminated with one of the raw chemicals used during its synthesis.

What is the *R*<sub>f</sub> value of the chemical?
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is**** B**** because:**

- X and Y **both** produce a spot at 0.18 cm which corresponds to pure paracetamol.
- The **impurity** in sample X is visible at 0.27 cm and this is the value which must be used to calculate the retention factor for the chemical.
- Use the equation for the retention factor: *R*<sub>f </sub>=  $\frac{distancetravelledbyspot}{distancetravelledbysolventfront}$
- R<sub>f</sub> = $\frac{0.27}{0.36}=0.75$

**A, C **and** D **are incorrect as these *R*<sub>f</sub> values are not correct.

parts.problem_md:
A mixture of sugars can be separated out by paper chromatography.

The student sprays the dried chromatogram with a locating agent.

Why is this used?
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****C**** because:**

- Sugars are colourless substances
- Locating agents are sprayed onto the chromatogram once the experiment has been carried out and allow the positions of the sugars to be observed

**A**, **B **and **D** are incorrect as these are not the purpose of the locating agent

choices.label: A
choices.text_md: To help the sugars dissolve in the solvent

choices.label: B
choices.text_md: To stop the sugars reacting with each other

choices.label: C
choices.text_md: To form coloured spots with the sugars

choices.label: D
choices.text_md: To aid the separation of the mixture

parts.problem_md:
The diagram below shows the apparatus a student used to separate a product from a reaction mixture.

![q5-medium-mcq-12-2-separation-purification-cie-igcse-chemistry](assets/005-q5-medium-mcq-12-2-separation-purification-cie-i.png)

What did the mixture contain?
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is**** B**** because:**

- The apparatus shown is for **distillation**.
- Distillation is used to **separate **two or more liquids from each other if they have **different boiling **points.
- The boiling point of ethanol is 78ºC and water is 100<sup>o</sup>C, ethanol therefore boils **before **the water does.
- It is then **cooled **and **condensed **back into the liquid form.

**A** is incorrect as filtration is the technique required for this mixture.

**C **and **D **are incorrect as aqueous and organic liquids are immiscible and so can be separated using a **separating funnel**.

choices.label: A
choices.text_md: Aqueous sodium chloride and unreacted solid catalyst

parts.problem_md:
A substance was analysed and was found to have a boiling point of 450 °C.

At room temperature it is a soft grey solid.

Which temperature could be the melting point of a pure sample of the substance?
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****D**** because**

- The substance is a **solid** at room temperature which is 20  °C.
- Its melting point must be above this temperature but must also be a **specific** number and **not a range** as the question states that the substance is pure.

**A** is incorrect as its melting point must be **above** room temperature so it has to be above 20 °C.

**B** and **C** are incorrect as pure substances boil at a **specific** temperature so their melting point would also be a specific temperature i.e. not a range of temperatures.

parts.problem_md:
Solid P melts at exactly 60<sup>o</sup>C and boils at exactly 310<sup>o</sup>C. Solid Q dissolves in ethanol and shows a green colour and a yellow colour when analysed using paper chromatography.

Which row is correct?

|   | **Contains only one substance** | **Contains more than one substance** |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | Q | P |
| **B** | Q | - |
| **C** | - | Q |
| **D** | P | Q |
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is**** D**** because:**

- Impure substances have melting points and boiling points that fall in a **range of  temperatures** while pure substances have **exact **and** sharp** melting and boiling  points.
- Solid P has an **exact** melting point and boiling point hence it is a pure substance.
- Paper chromatography of solid Q produces two spots, indicating it must contain more than one substance.

**A **and** B **are incorrect as solid Q contains **more than one** substance.

**C **is incorrect as solid P contains only** one** substance.

Which diagram correctly illustrates the filter paper at stage 3?

parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is**** A ****because: **

- The first fold requires that the filter paper adopts a** semi-circular shape**.
- This is then folded again to form a cone that fits inside the funnel.

**B**,** C **and** D **are incorrect as these diagrams do not correctly illustrate the final step to obtain the required shape.

parts.problem_md:
Pure H<sub>2</sub>O boils at 100 <sup>o</sup>C and freezes at 0 <sup>o</sup>C.

What is the melting point and boiling point of water after the addition of potassium chloride?

|   | Boiling point / <sup>o</sup>C | Freezing point / <sup>o</sup>C |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | 103 | -3 |
| **B** | 103 | 3 |
| **C** | 97 | -3 |
| **D** | 97 | No change |
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is**** A**** because:**

- Potassium chloride in water is an **impurity** which affects its physical properties.
- Pure water boils at 100 ºC and freezes at 0 ºC.
- In water, potassium chloride causes the boiling point to** increase **and the freezing point to **decrease**.
- This is why salt is used to prevent icing on roads as it lowers the freezing point, making it more difficult for ice to form at temperature close to 0 ºC.

**B **and** D **are incorrect as the freezing point of water **decreases **when potassium chloride is added to it.

**C **is incorrect as the boiling point of water **increases **when potassium chloride is added to it.

parts.problem_md:
The diagram below illustrates the experimental set-up to carry out distillation. What are the correct labels for points A and B on the condenser?

![q3-easy-mcq-12-2-separation-purification-cie-igcse-chemistry](assets/008-q3-easy-mcq-12-2-separation-purification-cie-igc.png)

|   | **Point A** | **Point B** |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | water in | water in |
| **B** | water in | water out |
| **C** | water out | water in |
| **D** | water out | water out |
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****B**** because:**

- Water enters at the bottom of the condenser in order to **fill** the entire condenser.
- It then flows out at the top once the condenser is **full** of water as shown in the diagram.

![ms3-easy-mcq-12-2-separation-purification-cie-igcse-chemistry](assets/009-ms3-easy-mcq-12-2-separation-purification-cie-ig.png)

**A**,** C **and** D **are incorrect as if the water enters at the top of the condenser it will pour straight out and the condenser would not fill up.

parts.problem_md:
A student performs a technique using the apparatus shown.

![q1-paper-1-nov-2020-ocr-gcse-chem](assets/010-q1-paper-1-nov-2020-ocr-gcse-chem.png)

Which separation technique has the student performed?
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****D**** because:**

- Filtration is the process of using a filter funnel and filter paper to separate an insoluble solid from a solution or liquid

  - The solid is unable to pass through the filter paper and becomes the residue
  - The solution / liquid that is collected in the flask is called the filtrate

**A**, **B** and **C** are incorrect as all three of these methods require heating

parts.problem_md:
Rocksalt is the mineral form of sodium chloride. It is known to commonly contain sodium chloride and sand along with other trace impurities.

A combination of physical changes and separation techniques can be used to produce higher purity sodium chloride and sand.

What is the correct order of physical changes and separation techniques to separate sodium chloride and sand?
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****C**** because:**

- Water is added to the rocksalt to dissolve the sodium chloride
- The mixture is then filtered to remove and separate the insoluble sand
- The filtrate contains sodium chloride dissolved in water
- The sodium chloride can be separated / removed from the water by crystallisation

**A** and **B** are incorrect as melting will not separate the sodium chloride, it will produce molten sodium chloride with sand mixed in

**D** is incorrect as dissolving gets the sodium chloride into solution but it still contains sand Subsequent crystallising then undoes this physical change

parts.problem_md:
Paper chromatography was used to determine if a banned preservative, X, is present in four samples obtained from four different packaged foods labelled A, B, C and D.

The results of the analysis of the foodstuffs are shown in the diagram below.

![q2-easy-mcq-12-2-separation-purification-cie-igcse-chemistry](assets/011-q2-easy-mcq-12-2-separation-purification-cie-igc.png)

Which foodstuff contains X?
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is**** B**** because:**

- Compare the chromatogram for X by using a ruler and carefully identifying the spots which are the same distance from the baseline as X.
- Only foodstuff **B** matches so B is the one that contains X.
- **A**, **C** and** D** do not match and so do not contain the banned dye.

**A, C **and** D **are incorrect as the chromatogram from these foodstuffs do not match with that of X and so do not contain the banned preservative.

parts.problem_md:
A student carries out an investigation on different plant extracts using paper chromatography. The experimental set-up he uses is shown below.

![q1-easy-mcq-12-2-separation-purification-cie-igcse-chemistry](assets/012-q1-easy-mcq-12-2-separation-purification-cie-igc.png)

Where should he place the samples of plant extract?
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is**** A**** because:**

- In paper chromatography the sample spots should all go onto the **base line**.
- This is always made with a** pencil **as to use ink would contaminate the samples being analysed.

**B **is incorrect as the samples would dissolve in the solvent.

**C **and** D** are incorrect as the base line is used to measure the distances to calculate the *R*<sub>f </sub>value. If the spots are above or below this line then the calculations will be **inaccurate**.

choices.label: B
choices.text_md: Below the pencil line in the solvent

choices.label: C
choices.text_md: Exactly 1 cm above the pencil line

choices.label: D
choices.text_md: Exactly 1 cm below the pencil line
